[vickys_yui]I’ve been exploring @termix_ai for a while now, yet I keep coming back to one question:
What will the economy look like when the participants are no longer humans, but AI "agents"?
For that to work, AI needs more than just intelligence. It requires a whole range of "grown-up" capabilities:
Identity: Who are you? Reputation: What is your track record? Discovery: What do you have to offer? Commerce: Who needs your services? Escrow: How are funds securely held? Verification: Is the task actually complete? Payment: Who gets paid?
That’s why I keep checking in on @termix_ai
What fascinates me isn't just the individual features, but how they all interconnect:
Identity verification → Discovery → Job acceptance → Escrow → Delivery → Inspection → Payment → Repeat.
If AI agents truly become "economic citizens" one day, this type of infrastructure will become increasingly vital.
It’s still early days, and there are plenty of questions regarding scalability.
But there’s one question I’m even more curious about: Can artificial intelligence... age?
I’m going to dig deeper into that one.
#TermiX_ai #AIAgents #AgentEconomy

[sheCodezArt]If you intend to get involved in the creation of AI videos, then one thing I would strongly advise learning is prompt engineering.
We don't have to become a kind of "prompt engineer" before we can use an AI video generator, rather it is essentially a matter of communication when producing good AI videos.
Even though a video generator can create a highly impressive scene in just a few seconds, that doesn't necessarily mean it has produced the scene as you imagined.
You could imagine a woman walking into a room, picking up her phone, getting a message, looking surprised and then turning towards the camera. But if you just ask an AI to create a scene of a woman walking into a room and looking surprised, it will have to make numerous decisions on your behalf.
What does she look like? What is she wearing? So, precisely where is she walking? What does the room look like? Where is the camera? Is it a wide shot or a close one? Is the camera with her or does it stay in one place? In which hand does she pick up the phone? What occurs before and what occurs after she gets the message? What sort of lighting is there in the room? At what speed should all this take place?
That is because the creation of videos by artificial intelligence is not merely a matter of producing pretty images that move; it is about directing a sequence of events.
That's where prompt engineering proves to be extremely useful.
The study of prompt engineering enables you to take an idea which is only loosely formed in your mind and break it down into instructions that an AI system can interpret more efficiently. To do this, you have to consider things such as the subject, the actions, the environment, the camera angles, the camera movements, the lighting, the composition, the timing, the transitions, the visual effects and the style together with continuity.
You also start to realize that the need to create a prompt does not mean that you have to write the longest prompt possible. Hell NO.
The true skill lies in identifying which information is important, in deciding how to organise it, in specifying what must be included, and in leaving what can be handled by the model.
Suppose you make a character in Scene 1; in Scene 2 you want the same character to be in a different location; in Scene 3 she is holding a phone; and in Scene 4 she is sitting in a car.
Suddenly, you are no longer just giving instructions for single videos. You're considering the consistency of the characters, their clothing, the setting, continuity, the use of the camera, and the way the story is told.
I believe that learning prompt engineering together with AI video creation is far more valuable than viewing prompting as a random assortment of "magic words" that you simply copy and paste into a generator.
Don't just learn prompts.
Find out how to direct AI.
After you've grasped that point, video-generation tools become a great deal more powerful since you're not merely having the AI produce something.

[YaseerGumel]Beyond Satellites: Real-Time 3D Data for Next-Gen Robotics
Modern geospatial data remains highly limited while satellites photograph roofs and mapping vehicle fleets log drivable roads
They leave the indoor and complex terrains that autonomous systems navigate such as loading docks, staircases and narrow market streets largely unmapped, vangrid bridges this gap through a crowdsourced bounty network where contributors record localized smartphone videos that are rendered into 3D models
Each recording receives an instant digital fingerprint anchored on the Base blockchain for transparent verification, this approach likely delivers the crucial infrastructure layer required for real world artificial intelligence
AI has plenty of internet data, but it’s still missing a massive chunk of real-world information, that’s a huge problem for robots trying to navigate environments that change every day @vangrid_io is tackling this with a crowdsourced network where people map spaces using their phones, creating verified data anchored on-chain
The concept is simple, when the real world changes, we need fresh data to feed into Physical AI, building better models doesn't mean much if the robots don't have an accurate, updated map of the room they are standing in.

item.title:
[karpathy]We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:
Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:
Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:
Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:
Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!
In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

[_The_Prophet__]⚡️The U.S. government is beginning to organize around superintelligence as a national capability before superintelligence even fully exists.
That is the signal.
States do this when they believe something is important enough that waiting for the market to sort itself out becomes strategically dangerous. Nuclear technology, space, semiconductors, energy, defense. Once the government creates a permanent coordinating apparatus around a technology, that technology has crossed from industry into state power.
The phrase “Super Intelligence Force” reveals the assumed end state. They are not organizing around chatbots or productivity software. They are organizing around the possibility that machine intelligence becomes one of the primary determinants of national power.
That means the race changes character.
AI companies still compete commercially, but the state increasingly cares about compute, models, energy, chips, infrastructure, security, talent, deployment, and who ultimately controls the frontier. Private AI development begins getting wrapped inside sovereign strategy.

The strangest part is that governments are now beginning to build institutions for a form of intelligence that could eventually exceed the cognitive capability of the institutions governing it.
That is historically unusual.
Human institutions are preparing to administer something potentially more intelligent than the humans inside them.
If this architecture persists, October 2026 may eventually look like the period when AI stopped being treated primarily as technology and started being treated as a new component of sovereignty.

[YIsah16]What if you could use AI without doing the boring work yourself?
That question got me curious about @ActionModelAI
Because think about how we use AI today.
“Write this.”
“Research that.”
“Give me the steps.”
AI gives you the answer.
Then you close the chat, open five tabs, click through a website, copy information, fill a form and do the actual work yourself.
That gap is what caught my attention.
Action Model is building Large Action Models (LAMs) around a simple shift:
Don’t just tell AI what to do. Let it take action.
A LAM can see what’s happening on a screen, decide what needs to happen next, interact with the interface, check the result and continue through a workflow.
That’s where Actionist comes in, turning this capability into something that can handle practical, multi step tasks.
But the part I kept coming back to wasn't just the automation.
It was the community.
People can contribute real interactions that help train the system, while the ecosystem is designed to let contributors participate in the value they help create.
And that changes the question.
We’re used to AI companies building models and everyone else simply using them.
What happens when the people helping build the intelligence can have a stake in the ecosystem too?
That’s the experiment I’m watching.
AI has spent years learning how to talk to us.
The next leap may be teaching it how to act.
And when that happens, the biggest change might not be smarter answers.
It might be fewer things we have to do ourselves.
